classification.tone: Grounded, anxious, darkly funny, and increasingly surreal

evaluation.positioning_hook: A panic-stricken college student discovers he can’t die and keeps rewinding time after a bus murder, forcing a relentless NYPD detective to decide whether he’s the killer or the only witness who matters.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is easy to grasp and has a clean commercial engine: a murder, a detective, and a young man trapped in a time-bending loop. The appeal is strongest for genre buyers and thriller audiences, with the college setting and dark humor widening the lane beyond straight procedural crime.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the cold open with the empty bus, the old woman with the Uzi, and the smash-cut reset that tells us the rules are broken. By the rooftop scene, the audience understands the central engine: Anthony is repeating time, Ji-a is the only one who can track it, and the case keeps erasing itself.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Anthony’s anxious, people-pleasing guilt and Ji-a’s hard-edged competence give the story two strong poles, and Joan adds a lively social counterweight. The roles are playable and actor-friendly, though the script is still mostly using them to drive the premise rather than fully opening their inner lives.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s boldest move is making time distortion feel like a murder-case contamination, with evidence disappearing, names shifting, and the detective’s memory becoming part of the mystery. The tonal choice to mix campus banter, noir investigation, and supernatural dread gives the material a sharper identity than a standard loop thriller.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The opening sequence is highly propulsive, and the investigation keeps producing new pressure points: missing evidence, erased cases, and the confrontation with XII. The momentum is strongest when the script is moving between Anthony and Ji-a; the middle section leans a bit more on setup than escalation, but the rooftop turn restores urgency.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a murder suspect whose crime scene can literally disappear from the record has a fresh inevitability to it. The clock-eye tattoo, the time-skipping antagonist, and the detective who alone notices the edits give the premise a memorable signature.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Queens Village, the NYPD precinct, the college campus, and the bus system all feel like parts of one connected urban machine, and the script uses those spaces to create procedural texture. The world is specific enough to generate story, especially through the bus routes, evidence locker, and campus bureaucracy, though it is still primarily serving the central mystery.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct voice: deadpan New York banter, sudden violence, and surreal time distortion all coexist without losing the emotional center. Joan’s profanity-laced warmth, Ji-a’s clipped authority, and XII’s playful menace create a tone that feels authored rather than generic.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the genre engine, there are clear reserves around guilt, identity, faith, and the pressure of being seen as a good person while fearing you are not. The script hints at a larger mythology through the clock-eye tattoo and the repeated erasures, and that suggests room for a deeper feature arc.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Anthony-Joan bond and the Ji-a-Larry friction give the script useful recurring dynamics, and Ji-a versus Joan has real scene energy. Still, the story is primarily powered by a few key pairings rather than a broad ensemble web.

casting_characteristics: Potentially recurring antagonist with stylized physicality

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with several exterior street/campus/bus-station scenes

technical.vfx_details: Time-reset moments, disappearance/erasure effects, and a few visual continuity distortions around the loop and clock imagery.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, blood hits, body effects, and practical reset continuity.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Streaming thriller / premium cable genre feature lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Festival-to-platform or streamer original feature release model

cost.note: Contemporary urban settings, limited company moves, and minor VFX keep this in a contained feature budget lane.

cast.note: The story centers on a small core of four leads with a handful of supporting roles and no child casting.

location.note: The script uses multiple New York locations, including bus, precinct, campus, dorm, rooftop, and street exteriors.

content.note: Gun violence, a body count, and repeated panic-driven violence push it into mature thriller territory.

rights.note: No named music, brands, or real-person references appear in the pages provided.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The premise turns a murder case into a memory war.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives a producer a clean hook with built-in escalation: the crime scene itself can be erased, rewritten, and re-litigated, which is a strong engine for a contained thriller. Genre buyers and streamers looking for a high-concept mystery with a fresh procedural wrinkle will immediately understand the value.
strengths.evidence: Ji-a discovers the evidence locker is empty, the case number no longer exists, and the clock-eye tattoo changes by a minute in her hand.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Anthony is a playable lead built on panic and guilt.
strengths.what_it_means: That creates a showcase role for an actor who can play fear, decency, and moral collapse in the same frame, which is exactly the kind of part that can elevate a genre package. Mid-career dramatic leads and younger breakout actors looking for a prestige-leaning thriller anchor would chase this.
strengths.evidence: He is introduced as a model student who can barely function, then confesses to Joan that he may have killed someone and later begs Ji-a to believe he is not lying.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Ji-a gives the story a hard, memorable procedural spine.
strengths.what_it_means: A detective who can track a case that keeps disappearing is a strong buyer asset because she turns the supernatural premise into an investigation rather than a pure concept exercise. Actors who specialize in controlled intensity and premium-cable authority roles will see a clear lane here.
strengths.evidence: Her clipped exchanges with forensics and Larry, plus the evidence-board sequence and rooftop confrontation, establish her as the story’s engine on the law-enforcement side.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone has a New York-specific snap.
strengths.what_it_means: The dialogue and setting give the script a lived-in urban texture that helps it stand apart from generic time-loop material and makes it easier to market as a specific city story. Buyers who respond to character-forward genre with voice — especially streamer and indie genre labels — will hear that immediately.
strengths.evidence: The bus stop, Queens Village, the precinct banter, and lines like 'Time. Place. Fuck off.' and 'Barry' create a very particular rhythm.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Joan is a strong pressure-release valve.
strengths.what_it_means: She gives the movie a social heartbeat and a source of humor that keeps the thriller from flattening into pure dread, which broadens audience access. Young-adult ensemble casting and actors with sharp comedic timing will be drawn to her fast, profane, loyal energy.
strengths.evidence: Her scenes with Anthony on campus and at the smoking spot give the script its most relaxed, human back-and-forth.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The antagonist arrives with a signature image.
strengths.what_it_means: XII’s clock-eye tattoo, chopped-cheese casualness, and time-skipping menace make the threat feel branded, which is valuable in a crowded genre marketplace. Performers who like scene-stealing, heightened antagonists will see a juicy role with a lot of attitude and control.
strengths.evidence: Her first full scene in Emma’s dorm room, where she explains the time-bending and casually demonstrates it by shooting Anthony and resetting the moment, is instantly legible.

whats_special.headline: This script has a clean, pitchable engine: a college student who can’t die, a detective whose case keeps getting erased, and a time-bending killer who turns every clue into a moving target. The result is a contained, character-forward thriller with a strong New York voice, a memorable visual signature, and a lead role actors will want to own.

lead_characters.name: Anthony Morgan
lead_characters.hook: Anthony is a high-achieving, deeply anxious college student whose default mode is politeness, overthinking, and self-erasure. He reads as the kind of young man who has spent his whole life trying to be good, which makes it devastating when the story forces him to confront the possibility that he may be something else entirely.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network — rapid internalization, verbal fragility, and a mind that never stops moving even when the body is frozen. It gives an actor the chance to play panic, guilt, and dawning supernatural terror while still keeping the audience emotionally attached to his decency.

lead_characters.name: Detective Ji-a Choi
lead_characters.demographics: Female · 30s to early 40s · Korean or Korean-American detective
lead_characters.hook: Ji-a is a hard-edged, hyper-competent detective who trusts process, pattern recognition, and her own instincts more than anyone in the room. She has the kind of clipped authority that makes every interaction feel like a test, but the script also lets her carry the loneliness of being the only person who can see the case changing in real time.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Jodie Foster in True Detective season 3 — controlled intelligence, moral pressure, and a detective whose authority is inseparable from her interior life. Actors who want a prestige procedural lead with steel, precision, and emotional containment will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Joan
lead_characters.hook: Joan is Anthony’s closest friend: sharp-tongued, funny, emotionally direct, and far more perceptive than she initially lets on. She brings the script its most human social rhythm, but she also carries the quiet ache of someone who knows more about Anthony than he is ready to say out loud.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Natasha Lyonne made feel electric in Russian Doll — fast comic timing with an undercurrent of loyalty and emotional intelligence. It gives an actor a chance to be the scene’s engine, the joke’s punchline, and the emotional witness all at once.

lead_characters.name: XII
lead_characters.demographics: Female · 20s to 30s · stylized, physically agile presence
lead_characters.hook: XII is a time-skipping predator with the confidence of someone who has already seen the end of the conversation and is amused by the middle. She is playful, threatening, and weirdly charismatic, with a streetwise voice that makes her feel both human and not-quite-human.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of scene-stealing antagonist territory that Tilda Swinton or Janelle Monáe has used to dominate genre material — a role where style, menace, and control are the performance. Actors who want to leave a mark with a memorable, high-concept villain will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Larry
lead_characters.hook: Larry is the earnest, slightly outmatched partner who keeps trying to be useful while Ji-a steamrolls past him. His comic frustration gives the procedural side some texture, and his confusion helps underline how abnormal the case really is.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that Ben Schwartz or Jake Johnson has turned into a scene-pop engine — fast talk, wounded pride, and comic timing inside a genre frame. It gives an actor a chance to be memorable without carrying the whole movie.

lead_characters.name: Emma
lead_characters.hook: Emma is more of a presence than a full social player in the pages provided, but she functions as a key emotional and narrative hinge through Joan’s connection to her and XII’s intrusion into her room. Her role is defined by absence, which makes her feel eerie and important.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of contained, high-impact role that can work like the quiet center of a scene in Hereditary or The Invitation — a performance built on stillness, vulnerability, and the audience’s awareness that something is off. Actors who like small but memorable genre parts will see the opportunity immediately.

lead_characters.name: Old Woman
lead_characters.hook: The Old Woman is a grotesquely cheerful assassin whose politeness and violence arrive in the same breath. She is memorable because she feels like a nightmare wearing the face of a commuter, and her giddy certainty gives the opening its shock value.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of left-field, unforgettable genre cameo that Kathy Bates or Margo Martindale has made iconic — a role that gets to be funny, terrifying, and instantly legible. Character actors who love a scene that detonates the movie will want it.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a grounded thriller where time distortion is felt through behavior, not spectacle.
director_appeal.fit_profile: First- or second-feature directors with a strong short-film reel, or established indie filmmakers who already work comfortably in performance-forward genre. This material rewards precision in blocking, rhythm, and tonal control more than big visual effects, so it suits directors who care about tension, urban texture, and actor-driven suspense.
director_appeal.detail: The script gives a director a clean playground for escalating dread through repetition, memory, and shifting point of view, while keeping the visual language contained enough to stay elegant. It will attract filmmakers who like genre stories that can be shot lean but still feel conceptually ambitious.

buyer_appeal.lane: Streamer thriller / premium genre feature lane
buyer_appeal.detail: The package can be built around one breakout lead and a strong supporting detective role, so it does not require a giant ensemble or heavy star stack to get moving. The contained urban footprint and minor VFX make it exportable and streamer-friendly, while the time-loop murder hook gives buyers a clean thumbnail and trailer concept.

considerations.area: Anthony’s inner conflict is strongest when it becomes action.
considerations.detail: The rooftop sequence already gives him a visible choice, and the next pass could keep looking for places where his fear turns into a decision rather than a confession. That would make the time-loop premise feel even more character-driven and would deepen the audience’s attachment to him.

considerations.area: The middle section leans on case explanation.
considerations.detail: The bus-station investigation, evidence-board material, and academic-advisor scene all do useful work, and one direction would be to let one of those information beats arrive through a sharper emotional turn. That would keep the mystery moving while preserving the script’s procedural clarity.

considerations.area: Ji-a and Larry can carry more independent energy.
considerations.detail: Their friction is already entertaining, and the version of the script where Larry’s competence or personal stake becomes more visible would give the detective side a richer secondary engine. That would also make the precinct feel less like a relay station and more like a living workplace.

considerations.area: The location footprint is manageable but varied.
considerations.detail: The story moves through the bus, precinct, campus, dorm, rooftop, and street exteriors, so a production pass should look for any places where two New York locations can be folded into one without changing the story beat. That would protect the urban specificity while keeping the shoot efficient.

considerations.area: The time-reset effects should stay elegant.
considerations.detail: The script only needs a handful of repeatable visual rules — the clock tick, the jump back, the erased evidence, the continuity snap — so the best version keeps those effects simple and consistent. That lets the movie spend its energy on performance and tension rather than on expensive visual invention.
